title: Opinion: Your game does not have to look like AI slop just because an AI drew stuff
author: AsparagusOk8818
selftext:
[This looks VERY AI](https://preview.redd.it/ic4nm9v1rcvh1.png?width=986&format=png&auto=webp&s=d45ee0158231cfe00c5bab43e47facf92565ad12)

  
...So, I've seen this said in response to some criticisms about the aesthetic of a game: 

'Of course it looks like AI slop, an AI drew it, there's nothing I can do, I am not an artist,' 

  
I posted that jungle canopy I image above as an obvious example of something that looks SO very AI. In a bad way. It's a jungle canopy parallax image generated with the following super simple prompt via ChatGPT's imagegen: 

'@create-image

1990s environmental belt-scroller pixel art.

A parallax background element that can infinitely scroll horizontally.

The treeline of a lush, dense jungle, seen at a distance. The jungle trees are tall and thick.'

...Now, someone can prove me wrong, but I don't think you could actually fix this by trying to use a more detailed prompt. Because the fundamental problem is that if you ask the AI to build a complex scene, the stable diffusion process it uses constructs that scene as a big blob first and then fills-in the blb with details. That's why it's so AI-looking; the issue is that you've got trees and foliage that in isolation are actually quite nice, but as a whole are just part of a big stupid blob. It looks like a random pile with a jungle plopped on top... because it is.

The same happens with city backgrounds, mountain backgrounds... you name it. And no amount of stylistic tailoring can solve the problem because it is fundamental to the process.

  
But you CAN fix it, and SHOULD fix it (IMHO): 

  
Build the background yourself using individual elements you ask the machine to draw. Don't ask it to build a city background, ask it for specific kinds of buildings and scenery. Then put it together yourself. Treat it like a slightly-more-frustrating lego set experience.

Sometimes you can even keep the assepts and re=use them, which will give your project a sense of place. 

If worldbuilding matters to you, this is also crucial to worldbuilding. Worlds aren't made of random building shapes or tree shapes or mountain shapes - they're filled with actual places and people. You should bring that intentionality with you. 

When you build the scene yourself using just elements that the AI drew to your specifications, it won't look like slop anymore... because it won't be. It'll be a scene you made using pieces you thoughtfully described to the machine. 

  
I think I am keeping that treeline just as a reminder to myself of this era, because after this era is gone nothing will draw like that again. No people will opt to and no machine will bother to. 

And I feel like it's worth preserving what a lot of stuff looked like for this very brief moment in time.

But you don't have to. It doesn't need to be and should not be an excuse. If you don't want your project to look like that, you don't need to just shrug at the prompt output of a scene that you have surrendered too much control and authorship over. Build the pieces separately and put them together by hand (or maybe Claude / Astra can also put them together for you? IDK, I haven't tried that).

replies.author: clockwork_blue
replies.body:
Remember the good old days before AI, when every game released was a masterpiece? You'd open the "New Releases" tab on Steam and find nothing but carefully crafted, beautifully polished games. You could only sit there in awe, wondering where all these Da Vincis were coming from.

Yeah, me neither.

In 2024 alone, Steam had around 18,000 game releases. That's roughly 1,500 games a month. How many of those did you actually play? A handful, probably, because the rest were already being filtered out by recommendations, reviews, word of mouth, and your own preferences.

I genuinely don't understand this sudden doomerism about AI "flooding the market with bad games." Have you guys actually been on Steam or any mobile app store in the past 15 years? The market has been drowning in shovelware, asset flips, and low-effort garbage for ages. AI didn't invent any of that.

People are acting like we're about to lose some golden age of quality control that never existed in the first place.

replies.author: NebbiaKnowsBest
replies.body:
I’m not saying we ever had this golden age of quality control or that everything released was perfect. 

I’m saying if we didn’t like it in its current state, it’s only going to get worse when more people can pump out more shit at a faster pace. I feel like that’s kinda obvious. If you have a bad system, introducing exponentially more bad into the system just makes the bad system worse. I don’t want the bad system, but I definitely don’t want a worse system. 

Do you think the ecosystem will be/has been improved recently? Do you have a way to filter and control that ecosystem? My point is that the tweet says people act like helpless bystanders but if you have no power to control how companies control the slop then you kind of are. 

Right now in your day to day life what actions could you take to not see anything made with ai on your feeds or in your steam store? Nothing, so you are a bystander. Slop happened to you. Respond to my actual point and not this random brigade you are on.

replies.author: clockwork_blue
replies.body:
You're assuming that more games being released means you'll somehow be forced to consume more bad games. That's not how it works. Steam already has thousands of games released every month, and you probably never even see 99% of them. You browse, filter, check reviews, follow recommendations, and play what interests you. Just like you always have.

And no, I don't need a magical "remove all AI" button any more than I need a "remove all asset flips" or "remove all Unity games" button. I care whether a game is good, not what tools the developer used to make it.

Your entire argument rests on the assumption that more content automatically makes discovery worse, as if recommendation systems and filtering can't evolve alongside the volume of releases.

If your definition of being a helpless bystander is that you can't personally control everything other people publish, then congratulations, you've been a helpless bystander since the invention of the internet.

replies.author: NebbiaKnowsBest
replies.body:
Dude where did I once say anything about being forced to consume more games? 

I already do those things as a consumer. This is not a consumer sub, it’s a dev sub. We have to think about not how we engage with the ecosystem but how potential players do. 

I’m not looking to control what people publish. I’m saying that “slop is happening to us” and we are not helpless bystanders because we chose to be, we are helpless bystanders because we cannot prevent it. 

Forget everything else you are trying to argue here because like I stated this has nothing to do with my thoughts on ai in development and just answer the question. Can you as a consumer prevent being fed slop right now? You can make an effort to not engage with it sure, but you cannot avoid it, so it is happening to you whether you like it or not. 

Also yes, more content does make discovery worse, that’s just maths. If I have 3 songs to pick from I can listen to 3 songs and pick my favourite. If I have 20094736519293 songs to listen to I physically cannot live long enough to listen to them all and pick a favourite. I’m not saying more choice is bad, but just logically flooding a market with content means it takes more time and effort to find the things you want.

replies.author: clockwork_blue
replies.body:
You're the one who brought up consumers, storefronts, and algorithms, so I'm not sure why this being a dev sub suddenly makes that perspective irrelevant.

Your song analogy assumes discovery is a linear process where you have to go through every available option to find something you like. Nobody does that. That's precisely why recommendation systems, reviews, communities, and curated lists exist. More content doesn't automatically mean proportionally more effort to discover something worthwhile.

Even at 150 new games a month, manually checking every release would already be tedious unless you made a habit of browsing daily. At 1,500, it becomes practically impossible. We've already crossed the point where discovery depends on filtering rather than manually exploring everything. Whether that number grows to 5,000 or 15,000, the underlying problem doesn't fundamentally change. Discovery systems need to scale with the volume of content, just as they have for years. Why are we suddenly assuming they won't be able to keep up?

And to answer the question you keep repeating: No, you can't prevent every piece of slop from appearing in your feed. You never could. But you're conflating exposure with consumption. Seeing a bad game in your recommendations doesn't mean you have to engage with it, let alone that it somehow prevents you from finding good games.

The barrier to entry has been dropping for decades, and every time it does, the bar for what makes a game stand out gets raised. AI is no different. Making it easier to produce a game doesn't magically make it easier to produce a *good* game.

You're assuming that more content inevitably means worse discovery, that filtering systems won't improve, and that consumers have no meaningful agency simply because they can't prevent every unwanted recommendation. That's a lot of assumptions to build an entire doomsday scenario around. This whole narrative of AI inevitably drowning everyone in slop and making good games impossible to discover is just doomerism dressed up as common sense.

comments.author: jamurai
comments.body: You can have AI draw better images, yes. It will rarely on its own. Once you get some good principals and learnings from the AI, have it write it down as a skill for future generations

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
Yeah, I'm not getting "slop" from this at all.  There's no weird errors where trees are overlapping incorrectly, there's no perspective issues, there's no objects blending into each other.

"Slop" is what happens when there's clear visual errors in individual pieces, and when you have a bunch of disparate styles from a bunch of disparate prompts just jammed together like you downloaded a bunch of asset packs from different people.  Art direction fixes "slop," not cutting your trees apart and manually stitching them back together just for the hell of it.

comments.author: robhanz
comments.body:
You picked a 90s video game background of a jungle.

Those tended to be tiled, and repetitive.

They tended to be palette limited, reducing depth.

And jungles generally mean "lots of trees".  Again, repetitive.

You picked one of the most repetitive things you could have done, and got.... something repetitive.

Also, ImageGPT2's default style tends to have a lot of "mottling" in it, which is very distinctive.

Gemini, on the other hand, did this, with the following prompt:

draw a pixel art background for a game that is scrollable with parallax, with varying forests and mountains and distant castles. 1920\*1080

By not specifying 90s, I got rid of the limited palette.  I specified a background with a greater selection of elements allowing for more natural variations.

https://preview.redd.it/0u4pmzlifdvh1.png?width=1024&format=png&auto=webp&s=3055d6c1e0f6d5450359d830f8c86da3578408bd

comments.author: Stalins_Ghost
comments.body:
There is a uniform detail or noise and a lack of heirarchy that is prevalent in AI art. Partially because ai 'artists' have a beginer understanding of design and because the assets are generated in isolation. Also the machine has little need for economy of work.

Human art is be more economic and wholistic in its approach, utilizing heirarchies to create readable and appealing designs. AI art in general always ends up looking over produced. this is not always because of AI but a lot of newcomers being new to design in general. 

To get AI art to look less 'AI' might require considering composition and heirarchy, intentionally genersting less detailed images in accordance with the composition.

That and AI does not feel broad in a shotgun approach so things always end up looking a certain way. It has only so much training data but I do find if you put in enough inputs it can go pretty far.

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
The grainy look is because of how the models interpret aliasing and image compression while training. The learn to incorporate compression artifacts into images that shouldn't have them, basically.

This image doesn't have any of that because it has been re-interpreted by a pixel snapper.

comments.author: gamerqc
comments.body:
Real talk.

If the game is good, you wouldn't care if it's made by AI. Or at least, you shouldn't. The sooner game devs understand this, the better. Most of them are pivoting away from slaving away at menial tasks. Spending weeks on modeling 3D props / creating art / products reviews / etc. will be a thing of the past very soon. It's much more cost-effective to reuse assets (see: RGG Studio/Pokémon) or generate basic models that you edit afterwards. 

Most of the biggest game studios are switching their processes to include AI or become AI-first. It's not a coincidence. People can bad mouth the tech all they want: the toothpaste isn't going back in the tube. It will lead to job loss and that sucks, but each new milestone in tech does. As long as human intervention is there, I don't see the problem at all. On the contrary, I think this will lead to the discovery of great games some people could have never created due to the high barrier of entry for this industry.

comments.author: Curious_Ad5417
comments.body: Agree with the building it from pieces part. I'm a solo dev on a dark fantasy keep builder and the town map was the thing that looked most like AI soup when I generated it as one image. What fixed it for me: every building is its own asset, placed by hand on a map I rendered in Blender, and the light and shadows come from that one scene, so everything sits in the same world. The monsters are image to 3D models that I rig and render as sprites, so they all share one camera angle and one light. Still AI underneath, but it reads as one place instead of a collage. The part that took longest was a fixed palette and a style sheet I paste into every prompt.

comments.author: zephyrion_drakon
comments.body: Try different tools like PixelLab or Midjourney. GPT Image is the worst for the "AI Slop" look I've found. What that look is, specifically, is a lack of discernment about where and how to place detail around the image, and a tendency to repeat the detail in a way that looks almost fractal-y. Other image models are not nearly as bad with this. I am personally fond of Midjourney's style. But unless you are using a pixel-art-specific generator the images you get will not be true "pixel art". They'll have a fake grid that cheats and doesn't downscale properly. But they can be good for references. I've gotten good results from using Midjourney for concepts, palettes, etc, then cropping and feeding those into PixelLab to get actual pixel art.
